docs/documentation/arbiters.html.title: Arbiters | Jitter2
docs/documentation/arbiters.html.summary: Arbiters An arbiter stores contact information for a pair of shapes. It holds up to four contact points and reuses them between simulation steps. CCD can create an arbiter before the shapes touch. Arbiters and shapes A body with several shapes can have several arbiters with the same opposing body, one for each shape pair in contact. For example, consider two bodies where body A has two box shapes and body B has one sphere shape. If both boxes overlap with the sphere, two separate arbiters are created: one for each box–sphere pair. Note One arbiter per shape pair The contact points can change while the arbiter remains the same. It lasts until contact ends or one of the shapes or bodies is removed. ArbiterKey Each arbiter is identified by an ArbiterKey, which is an ordered pair of ulong identifiers. For arbiters created by the engine, these identifiers are the ShapeId values of the two shapes involved. The shape with the smaller ID comes first. public readonly struct ArbiterKey(ulong key1, ulong key2) : IEquatable<ArbiterKey> { public readonly ulong Key1 = key1; public readonly ulong Key2 = key2; } The order of Key1 and Key2 matters for equality comparison. Accessing contact data The Arbiter class exposes a Handle property of type JHandle<ContactData>. Through arbiter.Handle.Data, the underlying contact information can be read and modified: ref ContactData data = ref arbiter.Handle.Data; ContactData has four contact slots. UsageMask identifies the valid slots. The structure also stores the pair's friction and restitution; each is the maximum of the two bodies' values. Caution Lifetime Obtain a fresh data reference each time you need one; do not retain it across simulation steps or world changes. Do not use an arbiter after it is removed or after its EndCollide callback, because it may be reused for another collision. Collision events The RigidBody class provides two events that supply the associated arbiter: body.BeginCollide += (Arbiter arb) => { // Called when a new arbiter is created involving this body. }; body.EndCollide += (Arbiter arb) => { // Called when this contact pair expires during a simulation step. }; BeginCollide can also occur for a predicted CCD contact before the shapes touch. EndCollide is raised when contact expires during a simulation step. Explicitly removing a body, shape, or arbiter does not raise EndCollide. Use these events to inspect contacts. For example, set friction when a contact pair begins: body.BeginCollide += (Arbiter arb) => { arb.Handle.Data.Friction = 0.0f; }; Since arbiters are per shape pair, a body with multiple shapes may trigger BeginCollide multiple times for the same opposing body—once for each shape pair. Custom arbiters Arbiters are not limited to the engine's built-in collision detection. Custom arbiters can be created and managed using world.GetOrCreateArbiter and world.RegisterContact. Creating an arbiter GetOrCreateArbiter takes two ulong identifiers and two rigid bodies. If an arbiter for the given ID pair already exists, it is returned; otherwise, a new one is created: world.GetOrCreateArbiter(id0, id1, body1, body2, out Arbiter arbiter); The identifiers do not have to be shape IDs—they can be any ulong values that uniquely identify the contact pair. This allows custom collision systems to create arbiters for application-specific purposes. Warning ID ordering The order of the two identifiers matters. ArbiterKey(1, 2) and ArbiterKey(2, 1) are considered different keys. When creating custom arbiters, be consistent with the ordering. Registering contacts Once an arbiter exists, contacts can be registered into it: world.RegisterContact(arbiter, point1, point2, normal); Supply both contact points in world space. The normal must be a unit vector pointing in the direction that pushes body 2 away from body 1. The optional removeFlags parameter disables parts of the response. For example, ContactData.SolveMode.Angular removes the angular response, leaving only linear motion. Alternatively, contacts can be registered using IDs directly, which also creates the arbiter if needed: world.RegisterContact(id0, id1, body1, body2, point1, point2, normal); Contact caching An arbiter keeps at most four contact points. A new point close to an existing one refreshes that contact and reuses its saved impulse. Otherwise it fills a free slot. When all slots are full, the engine chooses points that cover the touching region well. Contacts are removed when the shapes separate too far or the points slide too far apart. Reusing nearby contacts gives the solver a useful starting point on the next step. Arbiter lifecycle Creation: the engine creates an arbiter for a new shape pair, including predicted CCD contacts, and raises BeginCollide on both bodies. Update: each step adds or refreshes contact points and removes points that have separated too far. Removal: once contact ends, the engine raises EndCollide on both bodies and removes the arbiter. The arbiter object may then be reused for another pair.

docs/documentation/bodies.html.title: Rigid Bodies | Jitter2
docs/documentation/bodies.html.summary: Rigid Bodies A rigid body represents an object's position, rotation, mass, and motion. Attach shapes to define what it collides with. Creating a body Create a body in the world that will simulate it: var world = new World(); var body = world.CreateRigidBody(); Adding shapes A body can have more than one shape: body.AddShapes([new SphereShape(radius: 2), new BoxShape(size: 1)]); Shapes determine how bodies collide with each other. Warning Creating many bodies at once Set each body's position before adding shapes. Shapes enter collision detection immediately, so adding many at the origin creates unnecessary overlap checks. Warning Passing the same instance to multiple bodies Each shape instance can belong to only one body. Create a new instance for each body, or use Clone() on shape types that support it. Built-in primitives use their center of mass as the local origin, \((0, 0, 0)\). Adding a shape recalculates the body's mass and inertia from all its shapes, assuming a density of 1. Adding just a sphere body.AddShape(new SphereShape(radius: 1)); gives the body the mass and inertia of a sphere with radius 1 and density 1. The mass properties of the body can also be set directly using body.SetMassInertia. Inertia tensors use JSymmetricMatrix, which stores the six independent components of a symmetric matrix. Both body.InverseInertia and shape mass-property calculations use this type. body.SetMassInertia(JSymmetricMatrix.CreateScale(2, 3, 4), mass: 5); The tensor is expressed in body space, about the body's center of mass. Passing MassInertiaUpdateMode.Preserve to body.AddShape(...) or body.AddShapes(...) prevents the automatic recalculation of mass properties when shapes are added. Important The body's position represents its center of mass. Arrange its shapes so their combined center of mass is at the local origin, \((0, 0, 0)\). Use shape offsets when needed; see the teapot example. Debugging shapes Debug drawing shows the collision shapes attached to a body at their current positions and rotations. To display them, connect Jitter to your renderer by implementing IDebugDrawer: using Jitter2; using Jitter2.LinearMath; public sealed class PhysicsDebugDrawer : IDebugDrawer { public void DrawSegment(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, uint color) { // Draw a line from pA to pB using your renderer. // The positions are in world space; color is packed as 0xRRGGBBAA. } public void DrawTriangle(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, in JVector pC, uint color) { DrawSegment(pA, pB, color); DrawSegment(pB, pC, color); DrawSegment(pC, pA, color); } } Replace the comment in DrawSegment with a call to your renderer's line-drawing function. Create one drawer and reuse it: IDebugDrawer drawer = new PhysicsDebugDrawer(); Then call this in your application's drawing loop, after the physics step has completed: body.DebugDraw(drawer); Warning Debug drawing can be slow Drawing many bodies or using high detail settings can significantly reduce the frame rate. Point clouds and custom shapes can be especially expensive to draw. Limit debug drawing to the objects you need to inspect. This draws all shapes attached to body, including their offsets and rotations. The drawer above draws each triangle as three edges, producing a wireframe. For filled surfaces, call your renderer's triangle-drawing function in DrawTriangle; see shape drawing. The default drawing is white. To draw green shapes and make curved surfaces smoother: body.DebugDraw(drawer, new DebugDrawSettings { CurrentColor = DebugDrawColors.Green, Segments = 64 }); Spheres, capsules, cylinders, and cones are drawn using triangles. Segments sets the number of pieces around each circular cross-section; its default is 48. For example, Segments = 8 gives a cylinder an octagonal outline, while 64 makes it look much rounder. Higher values require more triangles. Boxes, triangle shapes, and convex hulls already have flat faces, so Segments has no effect on them. These settings affect only the visualization. PointCloudShape and custom shapes may use an approximate surface for debug drawing. See shape drawing for its limitations. Forces and impulses Forces and torques can be applied using body.AddForce. They accumulate until the next world.Step and are cleared at the end of that call. The resulting velocity change is applied during the following step. For a body initially at rest, with no gravity or other influences: body.AddForce(force); world.Step(dt); // Stores the velocity change; velocity and position are unchanged. world.Step(dt); // Applies the change to velocity and moves the body. This one-step delay also applies to gravity. Keep the timestep and substep count fixed: the velocity change is calculated using one step's substep duration and applied once per substep in the following step. For instantaneous velocity changes, use body.ApplyImpulse: // Linear impulse — changes velocity immediately. body.ApplyImpulse(new JVector(0, 10, 0)); // Impulse at a world-space position — changes both linear and angular velocity. body.ApplyImpulse(new JVector(0, 10, 0), hitPosition); Both overloads accept an optional wakeup parameter (default true). When set to false, the impulse is silently ignored if the body is sleeping. Gravity The gravity for the world can be set using world.Gravity. The property body.AffectedByGravity can be used to disable gravity for individual bodies. Gravity follows the force integration timing described above. Restricting motion and planar simulations body.AllowedMotion selects the directions in which a body can move and the axes around which it can rotate. The default, MotionAxes.All, allows all motion. Setting the property replaces the previous selection. All selected axes are in world space. For motion in the XY plane: body.AllowedMotion = MotionAxes.PlaneXY; // Equivalent to LinearX | LinearY | AngularZ. PlaneXZ and PlaneYZ provide the corresponding presets for the other coordinate planes. You can also combine individual axes: body.AllowedMotion = MotionAxes.LinearX | MotionAxes.AngularZ; An angular flag names the axis of rotation: AngularZ permits rotation around the world Z axis. MotionAxes.Linear permits all translations, and MotionAxes.Angular permits all rotations. Forces, impulses, contacts, and joints cannot move a body in a blocked direction. The restrictions also apply to kinematic velocities, but you can still set Position and Orientation directly. Restrictions preserve body.Mass and its body-space InverseInertia. If rotation around one axis affects rotation around another, locking an axis also changes the response around the remaining axes. Changing shapes or calling SetMassInertia updates mass properties without removing the restrictions. To allow all motion again: body.AllowedMotion = MotionAxes.All; Changing AllowedMotion stops motion in the blocked directions, clears saved contact and joint impulses, and schedules affected bodies to wake. Allowing motion again does not restore the old velocities. Gyroscopic forces are skipped while any axis is restricted. Do not change this property while another thread is stepping the world. MotionAxes.None blocks all simulated movement without changing the body's MotionType. The body still participates in contacts and connected groups. Use MotionType.Static for ordinary static geometry. Planar scenes still use 3D collision shapes. Bodies keep their initial position along the blocked axis, so place them in the same plane when building the scene. Custom constraints When writing a custom solver, use RigidBodyData.InverseMassVector for the inverse mass along each world axis. Calculate a linear velocity change with JVector.Multiply(data.InverseMassVector, impulse). Along a constraint direction, the inverse effective mass is JVector.Multiply(direction, data.InverseMassVector) * direction. JVector.Multiply multiplies matching components. The * operator between two vectors calculates a dot product, so it cannot replace that operation. RigidBodyData.InverseInertiaWorld is a JSymmetricMatrix stored in six scalars. It supports JVector.Transform and can be expanded to JMatrix using ToMatrix(). Custom solvers must handle zero response in prohibited directions, including singular effective-mass matrices. The body data occupies 128 bytes in single precision and 256 bytes in double precision. Access its fields by name rather than relying on field offsets. An effective-mass matrix can be singular when motion is blocked. For symmetric, positive-semidefinite matrices, MathHelper.PseudoInverseSymmetric calculates an inverse for the allowed motion and leaves blocked directions at zero: JMatrix effectiveMass = MathHelper.PseudoInverseSymmetric(inverseEffectiveMass); Compute this during constraint preparation and reuse the result in solver iterations. The method assumes finite, symmetric, positive-semidefinite input. It uses a numerical cutoff when diagonalizing singular or nearly singular matrices; see its API documentation for the precision-dependent tolerance. Damping Damping gradually slows a body's motion. Set the linear and angular factors with body.Damping; zero disables damping and one stops that motion. Each call to world.Step multiplies velocity by \(1-\gamma\), where \(\gamma\) is the corresponding damping factor. Damping is applied per step, so smaller time steps produce more damping over the same elapsed time. Continuous collision detection Continuous collision detection (CCD) helps prevent fast-moving or rotating bodies from passing through obstacles between simulation steps. Enable it with body.EnableCcd = true. When two bodies both move quickly, enable CCD on both, for example two fast projectiles. A moving body without CCD can otherwise be missed. CCD predicts collisions from both movement and rotation. A collision response can change that prediction, so Jitter checks again using the new velocities. It also checks bodies set in motion by those responses, even if they did not have CCD enabled. Three world settings control the cost and behavior: CcdIterations: number of collision discovery passes. More passes can find additional collisions but cost more. Default is 4. CcdVelocityThreshold: pairs below this estimated relative surface speed skip CCD checks. The estimate includes translation and rotation. Default is 0.1 world units per second. CcdRelaxationFactor: fraction of the predicted gap that a contact allows to close during one step. Default is 0.9, leaving a small separation margin. A fixed number of passes cannot guarantee that every collision is found. Joints are solved afterward and can change motion again. Smaller time steps may still be needed. Friction and Restitution Friction and restitution coefficients may be set through body.Friction and body.Restitution. For a collision of two bodies with different coefficients the maximum value of each body is taken. Collide events RigidBody provides two events: BeginCollide and EndCollide. BeginCollide is raised when a contact pair begins, including a predicted CCD contact. EndCollide is raised when that pair expires during a simulation step; explicit removal does not raise it. See Arbiters for details and examples. Activation/Deactivation Bodies connected through contacts or constraints form an island. These groups go to sleep and wake together. A body is ready to sleep once its linear and angular speeds stay below body.DeactivationThreshold for body.DeactivationTime seconds. When all non-static bodies in an island are ready, the island sleeps. Sleeping bodies have very little simulation cost and can wake when they collide with an active body. body.SetActivationState(true) requests a wake-up on the next step. Passing false requests sleep, but a body that is still moving too fast, or is connected to an active body, can stay awake. The call does not immediately change body.IsActive. For explicit immediate deactivation, use world.ForceSleepIsland(island). This deactivates the whole island at once, ignores the normal deactivation thresholds, and clears linear velocity, angular velocity, queued forces, and queued torques for all bodies in the island. Activation state is most meaningful for dynamic and kinematic bodies: Dynamic bodies are actively simulated while awake and skipped while sleeping. Kinematic bodies can be part of islands. They are treated as infinite-mass bodies by the solver, but they can wake connected dynamic bodies through contacts or constraints. Static bodies remain inactive and do not connect islands. Calling body.SetActivationState(true) does not activate the static body itself. Static bodies Static bodies (body.MotionType == MotionType.Static) have infinite mass and therefore are not affected by collisions or constraints. They also do not join islands. Static bodies do not generate collisions with other static or inactive bodies. Static bodies are normally inactive even if body.SetActivationState(true) is called. Changing a static body's position or orientation updates its collision bounds and wakes affected non-static bodies on the next step. The static body stays inactive. Use this for occasional edits to level geometry; use a kinematic body for a platform or obstacle that moves continuously. Kinematic bodies Kinematic bodies (body.MotionType == MotionType.Kinematic) move according to their assigned linear and angular velocities. Forces, collisions, and constraints do not change those velocities. They can push dynamic bodies and take part in island activation and sleeping.

docs/documentation/constraints.html.title: Constraints | Jitter2
docs/documentation/constraints.html.summary: Constraints Constraints limit how two bodies can move relative to each other. A joint combines constraints into a familiar connection, such as a hinge or a weld. For a complete example with two boxes, a hinge, and a debug drawer, follow the Hinge tutorial. Degrees of Freedom A body can move along three axes and rotate around three axes. These are its six degrees of freedom (DOF). A constraint restricts one or more of them. Constraint Removed DOF Description BallSocket 3 translational Anchors a point on each body together FixedAngle 3 rotational Locks relative orientation between bodies HingeAngle 2 rotational (3 with limit) Allows rotation around a single axis only, optionally enforces angular limits PointOnLine 2 translational (3 with limit) Constrains a point to a line, optionally limits distance along the axis PointOnPlane 1 translational (when limit active) Keeps an anchor on a plane or within a range of distances from it DistanceLimit 1 translational (when limit active) Constrains the distance between anchor points, only enforced when outside the limit range TwistAngle 1 rotational (when limit active) Limits relative twist around an axis, only enforced when outside the limit range ConeLimit 1 rotational (when limit active) Limits angular tilt between two axes EllipticalConeLimit 1 rotational (when limit active) Limits swing between inner and outer elliptical cones; leaves twist free AngularMotor — Drives angular velocity (does not remove DOF) LinearMotor — Drives linear velocity (does not remove DOF) SpringConstraint 1 translational Spring-like force along the anchor connection Joints Joints are combinations of constraints for common use cases: Joint Constraints used Remaining DOF HingeJoint BallSocket + HingeAngle (+ optional AngularMotor or TwistServo) 1 rotational PrismaticJoint PointOnLine + FixedAngle or HingeAngle (+ optional LinearMotor or LinearAxisServo) 1 translational; also 1 rotational when pinned is false UniversalJoint BallSocket + TwistAngle (+ optional AngularMotor or AngularServo) 2 rotational WeldJoint BallSocket + FixedAngle 0 (fully locked) Joint drives HingeJoint, PrismaticJoint, and UniversalJoint can create an optional motor or servo. Use JointDrive.Motor to control speed or JointDrive.Servo to reach a target position or angle. Omit the drive, or use JointDrive.None, for an undriven joint. var elbow = new HingeJoint( world, upperArm, lowerArm, center, axis, angle: AngularLimit.FromDegree(0, 135), drive: JointDrive.Servo); elbow.Servo!.TargetAngle = JAngle.FromDegree(90); elbow.Servo.MaximumTorque = 20; A hinge's Servo is a TwistServo. Its target uses the same zero angle and positive rotation direction as the hinge's HingeAngle.Angle. A prismatic joint's Servo is a LinearAxisServo. Its target position uses the same zero and direction as the joint's Slider.Distance: var slider = new PrismaticJoint( world, body1, body2, center, axis, limit: new LinearLimit(0, 2), drive: JointDrive.Servo); slider.Servo!.TargetPosition = 1.5f; slider.Servo.MaximumForce = 100; A universal joint's Servo is an AngularServo. Its target is the orientation of body 2 relative to body 1. Initially, it holds their current relative orientation: var universal = new UniversalJoint( world, body1, body2, center, axis1, axis2, drive: JointDrive.Servo); universal.Servo!.TargetRelativeOrientation = targetRelativeOrientation; universal.Servo.MaximumTorque = 20; The twist constraint remains active, so only orientations allowed by the joint can be reached. Drives start with a maximum force or torque of zero. Set this limit to make the drive act. The drive does not replace the joint's mechanical limits. Enabling, disabling, removing, or drawing the joint also applies to its drive. The Motor property is non-null only with JointDrive.Motor; Servo is non-null only with JointDrive.Servo. The older hasMotor constructor overloads are obsolete and remain supported. Replace hasMotor: true with drive: JointDrive.Motor, or omit the drive when no motor is needed. Creating constraints Create constraints through the world: var constraint = world.CreateConstraint<ConstraintType>(body1, body2); Jitter2 allocates and assigns unmanaged memory to constraints internally, allowing them to be used like regular classes. The solver interacts with unmanaged memory structures of type ConstraintData (256 bytes) or SmallConstraintData (128 bytes), depending on whether constraint.IsSmallConstraint is set. Small constraints are designed for simpler constraints with a smaller memory footprint, such as spring constraints for soft bodies. Caution Constraint Initialization For all default constraints, constraint.Initialize must be called once after world.CreateConstraint. World space initialization Supply anchor points and axes in world coordinates. Most constraints use the bodies' current positions and orientations as their reference, so arrange the bodies as intended before calling Initialize. The anchors and axes then move with their respective bodies. Servos can instead be initialized with a target they have not yet reached. Example: Hinge joint For a swinging door, BallSocket keeps the hinge anchors together and HingeAngle allows rotation around the hinge axis: var hingeAngle = world.CreateConstraint<HingeAngle>(body1, body2); hingeAngle.Initialize(hingeAxis, AngularLimit.Full); var ballSocket = world.CreateConstraint<BallSocket>(body1, body2); ballSocket.Initialize(hingeCenter); Alternatively, the HingeJoint can be used for convenience: var hinge = new HingeJoint(world, body1, body2, hingeCenter, hingeAxis); Cone limits ConeLimit restricts the angle between two axes to a range from 0° to 180°. Ranges such as [0°, 45°], [135°, 180°], and [0°, 180°] are valid. Equal limits fix the angle when it lies strictly between 0° and 180°, for example [30°, 30°]. The fixed ranges [0°, 0°] and [180°, 180°] are rejected by Initialize and the Limit property. To keep axes parallel or antiparallel while allowing free twist, use HingeAngle with AngularLimit.Full: var hingeAngle = world.CreateConstraint<HingeAngle>(body1, body2); hingeAngle.Initialize(hingeAxis, AngularLimit.Full); Position the bodies with the intended axes aligned or antiparallel before initialization. HingeAngle stores their current relative orientation as its reference; it does not pull two arbitrarily misaligned axes into alignment during initialization. Elliptical cone limits EllipticalConeLimit allows different tilt limits in two perpendicular directions. The cone is attached to body 1 and limits an axis attached to body 2. Supply the directions in world space; they will rotate with their respective bodies. var cone = world.CreateConstraint<EllipticalConeLimit>(body1, body2); cone.Initialize( axis: JVector.UnitY, referenceDirection: JVector.UnitX, limitAlongReference: AngularLimit.FromDegree(15, 60), limitAlongPerpendicular: AngularLimit.FromDegree(5, 25)); The lower bounds define the inner ellipse (15° and 5°); the upper bounds define the outer ellipse (60° and 25°). Swing is allowed between these boundaries. Setting both lower bounds to zero removes the inner boundary. Setting each lower bound equal to its upper bound constrains swing to one elliptical cone surface. Identical ranges in both directions give a circular cone. The limits form an ellipse, rather than two independent angle limits. Tilting partway toward one limit leaves less room in the perpendicular direction. GetSwing returns these two tilt components, measured along the reference direction and axis cross referenceDirection. Each boundary satisfies (swing1 / angle1)^2 + (swing2 / angle2)^2 = 1. The reference direction is projected onto the plane perpendicular to the cone axis. A direction parallel to the axis is rejected. Each range must satisfy 0 <= From <= To < 180°, with a positive upper bound. The lower bounds must either both be zero or both be positive. Fixed zero and 180° tilt are unsupported. Change the ranges together using SetLimits; inspect the current coordinates using GetSwing. The two-axis Initialize overload supports an initially tilted body 2. The single-axis overload starts at zero tilt, which violates a positive inner boundary and will be corrected by the solver. Translation and twist of body 2 about its constrained axis remain free. Combine this constraint with BallSocket for a joint, and optionally TwistAngle to limit twist. Servos Servos drive bodies toward a target configuration. They can start outside that configuration, and their targets can change between simulation steps. Changing a target wakes sleeping connected dynamic bodies on the next step. Motors control velocity; servos control position or orientation. Servo Controls Target AngularServo 3 angular directions TargetRelativeOrientation: body 2's orientation in body 1's frame TwistServo 1 angular direction TargetAngle: twist relative to the initial zero-twist pose LinearServo 3 linear directions TargetPosition: offset from anchor 1 to anchor 2, in body 1's frame LinearAxisServo 1 linear direction TargetPosition: signed anchor separation along the axis attached to body 1 Maximum force or torque defaults to zero, as with motors. Set MaximumForce or MaximumTorque to enable the drive. Positive infinity allows unlimited force or torque. Bias controls how quickly the servo corrects its error. Higher Softness lets it yield more under load. For example, drive two robot arm segments toward a relative orientation: var servo = world.CreateConstraint<AngularServo>(upperArm, lowerArm); servo.Initialize(JQuaternion.CreateRotationX(0.5f)); servo.MaximumTorque = 20; // Choose a different configuration later without moving the bodies directly. servo.TargetRelativeOrientation = JQuaternion.CreateRotationX(1.0f); The parameterless AngularServo.Initialize() captures the current relative orientation instead. LinearServo.Initialize(anchor1, anchor2) accepts separate world-space attachment points; its default target of zero pulls them together. LinearAxisServo.Initialize also accepts the desired signed separation. TwistServo.Initialize accepts a target angle relative to its initial reference, so a nonzero target begins with an angular error. TwistServo uses signed joint angles from -180° to +180°. Moving from -170° to +170° travels 340° through zero. Targets outside this interval are rejected; revolutions are not tracked. Use mechanical limits to keep the joint's motion inside the angular interval. AngularServo targets an orientation and uses the shortest rotation to reach it, so equivalent orientations represent the same target. Servos act alongside mechanical constraints. For an elbow, use a hinge to keep the arm segments connected and enforce the joint's angle limits, then add a TwistServo around the same axis. Its torque limit controls the actuator's strength while the hinge retains its mechanical limits. Fixed constraints To constrain a rigid body relative to world space, use world.NullBody as one of the bodies. For example, to keep a capsule upright: var upright = world.CreateConstraint<HingeAngle>(capsule, world.NullBody); upright.Initialize(JVector.UnitY, AngularLimit.Full); Softness and Bias Bias controls how quickly a constraint corrects position or angle errors. Higher Softness lets the constraint yield more under load, which can improve stability at the cost of accuracy. Substeps can also improve joint stability. Enable/Disable constraints Constraints can be temporarily enabled or disabled using constraint.IsEnabled. Debug drawing Constraints and joints can draw their anchors, axes, and limits through an IDebugDrawer: constraint.DebugDraw(drawer); joint.DebugDraw(drawer); See setting up a debug drawer to connect this to your renderer. Call these methods after the physics step, while the world is not being modified by another thread. Green shows reference guides and upper or fixed limits, red shows lower limits, and white shows current anchors and directions. Coordinate frames use red for X, green for Y, and blue for Z. Constraint Reading the drawing BallSocket The two anchor markers should coincide. The line between them shows separation. DistanceLimit Spheres around the first anchor show the allowed distances to the second anchor. PointOnLine Crosses mark stops along the line; arrows mark unbounded ends. A white line shows displacement away from the line. PointOnPlane Grids show the limiting planes. A white projection line appears when the anchor is outside the allowed region. The planes extend beyond the grids. ConeLimit, EllipticalConeLimit The white axis must stay within the outer cone and outside any red inner cone. Equal limits allow motion along one cone surface. HingeAngle An arc shows the allowed angles, or a green ray marks a fixed angle. The white ray shows the current angle. Short axis arrows reveal hinge misalignment. TwistAngle The dial shows the current twist and its limits. The white axis shows the current body direction; swing remains free. FixedAngle Each body has a coordinate frame adjusted for the initial relative orientation. Corresponding axes stay parallel when the constraint is satisfied. No frame is drawn for World.NullBody. LinearMotor Green arrows show body 1's contribution and white arrows show body 2's contribution to the requested relative motion. These show target direction, not measured velocity; a static body stays still. AngularMotor A green circle and white arrow show the target rotation of body 2, or body 1 when body 2 is static or kinematic. Short lines show both motor axes. The arrow shows target direction, not measured speed; a zero target has no arrow. AngularServo A green target frame and an RGB current frame share an origin. Corresponding axes align when the target is reached. TwistServo The dial marks the target twist and the current twist angle. LinearServo Green and white markers show the target and current anchor positions; the connecting line shows the position error. LinearAxisServo Markers show target and current position projected onto the reference axis. Perpendicular motion is uncontrolled. SpringConstraint The coil joins the anchors; the green cross marks the rest length along the spring direction. Pass DebugDrawSettings to change the appearance: constraint.DebugDraw(drawer, new DebugDrawSettings { GuideSize = 2, FrameSize = 1.5f }); GuideSize changes the size of guides. FrameSize sets the length of coordinate-frame axes in world units, and PointRadius sets the radius of anchor spheres. Arrowhead size and shaft thickness are adjusted separately using ArrowHeadSize and ArrowShaftRadius. Physical distances and angular limits keep their actual values. See DebugDrawSettings for color, arrow, and detail settings. Arrows are solid by default. Set SolidArrows = false for wire arrows. ArrowSegments controls how round arrowheads and shafts look. Your drawer's DrawTriangle implementation controls whether solid arrows and anchor markers appear filled or as triangle edges. When drawing your own guides, DrawArrow and DrawFrame use the same defaults; DrawWireArrow and DrawWireFrame explicitly draw wire geometry. Constraint lifetime Removing a constraint makes its simulation data unavailable. This also happens automatically when: either connected body is removed; world.Clear() removes the connected bodies; or the world is disposed. Changing a body's motion type does not remove the constraint. It is suspended while neither connected body is dynamic. Check constraint.IsValid before using a reference that may have been removed: world.Remove(body1); // also removes constraints attached to body1 if (constraint.IsValid) { constraint.IsEnabled = false; } If IsValid is false, do not use properties or methods that access the constraint's simulation data. Rigid bodies have the same body.IsValid check after removal or world disposal. Use World.ConstraintRemoved to clean up application data when a constraint is removed: world.ConstraintRemoved += removedConstraint => { // Drop any application-side state associated with removedConstraint. }; The constraint is already invalid when the callback runs. Disabling a constraint and disposing the world do not raise this event.

docs/documentation/dynamictree.html.title: Dynamic Tree | Jitter2
docs/documentation/dynamictree.html.summary: Dynamic Tree The dynamic tree finds objects whose axis-aligned bounding boxes overlap. These boxes have edges parallel to the world axes and are often called AABBs. An object tracked by the tree is called a proxy and implements IDynamicTreeProxy. The tree groups nearby boxes so a query can skip whole groups that are out of range. Slightly expanded boxes also let objects move a short distance without needing to be reinserted every time. Adding proxies All shapes added to a rigid body (body.AddShape) are automatically registered with world.DynamicTree. Custom implementations of IDynamicTreeProxy can be added to the tree using tree.AddProxy. In this case, a BroadPhaseFilter must be implemented and registered (using world.BroadPhaseFilter) to handle collisions with the custom proxy, otherwise an InvalidCollisionTypeException is thrown. Enumerate Overlaps Call tree.Update to refresh moving objects and the set of overlapping pairs. world.Step does this automatically for world.DynamicTree. Use tree.EnumerateOverlaps to visit those pairs; overlapping boxes do not necessarily mean the shapes touch. After changing a shape's geometry, call world.DynamicTree.Update(shape) to refresh it immediately. See Changing an attached shape for the other updates needed. Querying the tree Choose a query based on the result you need: Query(...) tests bounding boxes and returns objects that might intersect the query. RayCast(...), SweepCast(...), and FindNearest(...) also test the shapes and return the nearest accepted result. Broadphase-only queries Find objects whose tree bounds overlap a box: public void Query<T>(T hits, in JBoundingBox box) where T : class, ICollection<IDynamicTreeProxy> public void Query<TSink>(ref TSink hits, in JBoundingBox box) where TSink : ISink<IDynamicTreeProxy> Or find objects whose tree bounds intersect a ray: public void Query<T>(T hits, in JVector rayOrigin, in JVector rayDirection) where T : class, ICollection<IDynamicTreeProxy> public void Query<TSink>(ref TSink hits, in JVector rayOrigin, in JVector rayDirection) where TSink : ISink<IDynamicTreeProxy> For a custom query, you can traverse tree.Nodes directly. This example finds bounding boxes containing a point. Only run it on a nonempty tree (tree.Root >= 0): var stack = new Stack<int>(); stack.Push(tree.Root); ReadOnlySpan<DynamicTree.Node> nodes = tree.Nodes; while (stack.TryPop(out int id)) { ref readonly DynamicTree.Node node = ref nodes[id]; if (node.ExpandedBox.Contains(point)) { if (node.IsLeaf) { Console.WriteLine($"{node.Proxy} has a bounding box containing {point}."); } else { stack.Push(node.Left); stack.Push(node.Right); } } } Exact query helpers These methods use the tree to find candidates, then test their shapes. They return true when an accepted result is found and false otherwise. Ray casting All proxies implementing IRayCastable can be ray cast, including all shapes: // Unbounded public bool RayCast(JVector origin, JVector direction, RayCastFilterPre? pre, RayCastFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector normal, out float lambda) // Bounded: only considers hits with lambda < maxLambda public bool RayCast(JVector origin, JVector direction, float maxLambda, RayCastFilterPre? pre, RayCastFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector normal, out float lambda) The ray starts at origin and extends along direction, which need not be normalized. The hit point is origin + lambda * direction. With a unit direction, lambda is the distance to the hit. The method also returns true when the origin is inside a shape; in that case lambda is zero and normal is JVector.Zero. Use the pre- and post-filters to skip unwanted objects or hits. Sweep casting All proxies implementing ISweepTestable can be sweep-tested, including all shapes: // Unbounded public bool SweepCast<T>(in T support, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, in JVector direction, SweepCastFilterPre? pre, SweepCastFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector pointA, out JVector pointB, out JVector normal, out float lambda) where T : ISupportMappable // Bounded: only considers hits with lambda ≤ maxLambda public bool SweepCast<T>(in T support, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, in JVector direction, float maxLambda, SweepCastFilterPre? pre, SweepCastFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector pointA, out JVector pointB, out JVector normal, out float lambda) where T : ISupportMappable Pass the convex query shape with its world-space orientation and position. It moves along direction without rotating. Its position at impact is position + lambda * direction. For a sweep over a fixed distance, set direction to the full displacement and use maxLambda = 1. pointA is a point on the query shape at its starting position. Move it to the impact position with pointA + lambda * direction. The target stays stationary during the query, so pointB is already its world-space contact point. normal is also in world space. If the shapes already overlap, the result is true, lambda is zero, and normal is JVector.Zero. Contact points are undefined in that case. The pre-filter (SweepCastFilterPre) receives a candidate before its shape is tested. Use it to ignore objects, such as the body being swept. The post-filter (SweepCastFilterPost) receives the full SweepCastResult, including Lambda, Normal, PointA, and PointB. Use it to inspect the geometry of a hit. Returning false skips that result and continues the search. You can also collect results here and return false to keep searching. For common built-in query shapes, convenience overloads are available: public bool SweepCastSphere(float radius, in JVector position, in JVector direction, ...) public bool SweepCastBox(in JVector halfExtents, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, in JVector direction, ...) public bool SweepCastCapsule(float radius, float halfLength, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, in JVector direction, ...) public bool SweepCastCylinder(float radius, float halfHeight, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, in JVector direction, ...) Each has a bounded variant with a maxLambda parameter. For a shape that also rotates, use the overload with linear velocity, angular velocity, and a time limit: bool hit = tree.SweepCast(shape, orientation, position, velocity, angularVelocity, maximumTime, pre, post, out var proxy, out var pointA, out var pointB, out var normal, out var time); angularVelocity is a world-space vector in radians per second. The shape rotates about position while that origin moves with velocity. maximumTime must be finite and nonnegative; the returned time is in seconds. Targets stay at their current poses during the query. This overload supports all built-in shapes. Custom proxies can participate by implementing IAngularSweepTestable. With zero angular velocity, it uses the existing translation-only cast. The filters work as above. Contact points still refer to the initial poses, so pointA must be rotated about the initial position as well as translated to reach the impact pose. pointB is already at the impact point because the target stays fixed. A numerical search that cannot finish does not report a hit. Find nearest query All proxies implementing IDistanceTestable can be distance-queried, including all shapes: // Unbounded: considers all IDistanceTestable proxies in the tree public bool FindNearest<T>(in T support, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, FindNearestFilterPre? pre, FindNearestFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector pointA, out JVector pointB, out JVector normal, out float distance) where T : ISupportMappable // Bounded: only considers proxies within maxDistance public bool FindNearest<T>(in T support, in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, float maxDistance, FindNearestFilterPre? pre, FindNearestFilterPost? post, out IDynamicTreeProxy? proxy, out JVector pointA, out JVector pointB, out JVector normal, out float distance) where T : ISupportMappable The query shape is defined by an ISupportMappable plus its world-space orientation and position. pointA and pointB are the closest points on the query shape and the found object, in world space. normal is a unit vector pointing from the query shape toward that object. An overlapping object also counts as a result. In that case distance is zero, normal is JVector.Zero, and the closest points are undefined. The method returns false when no accepted object is found within range. The pre-filter (FindNearestFilterPre) receives a candidate before its shape is tested. The post-filter (FindNearestFilterPost) receives the calculated FindNearestResult. Return false from either to skip that candidate and continue searching. To skip overlapping proxies and find the nearest separated proxy instead, reject overlap results in the post-filter: world.DynamicTree.FindNearestSphere(radius, position, pre: null, post: result => result.Distance > 0, out proxy, out pointA, out pointB, out normal, out distance); For common built-in query shapes, convenience overloads are available: public bool FindNearestPoint(in JVector position, ...) public bool FindNearestSphere(float radius, in JVector position, ...) Each has a bounded variant with a maxDistance parameter. Overlap check example To find shapes overlapping a sphere, first query its bounding box, then test each candidate against the sphere: // Returns all RigidBodyShapes overlapping a sphere at 'center' with 'radius'. static IEnumerable<RigidBodyShape> OverlapSphere(World world, JVector center, float radius) { var queryBox = new JBoundingBox( center - new JVector(radius), center + new JVector(radius)); var candidates = new List<IDynamicTreeProxy>(); world.DynamicTree.Query(candidates, queryBox); var querySphere = SupportPrimitives.CreateSphere(radius); foreach (var proxy in candidates) { if (proxy is not RigidBodyShape shape) continue; ref var data = ref shape.RigidBody.Data; bool hit = NarrowPhase.Overlap( querySphere, shape, JQuaternion.Identity, data.Orientation, center, data.Position); if (hit) yield return shape; } } The bounding-box query limits the work; NarrowPhase.Overlap removes candidates whose boxes overlap but whose shapes do not.

docs/documentation/filters.html.title: Collision Filters | Jitter2
docs/documentation/filters.html.summary: Collision Filters Collision filters let you skip selected collisions or adjust contact information. They run at three stages: Filter When it runs Use it to world.DynamicTree.Filter When the tree considers a pair of objects Exclude pairs from collision detection. world.BroadPhaseFilter Before testing the shapes for contact Apply collision groups or handle custom objects. world.NarrowPhaseFilter After contact points are found Reject a collision or adjust its contact information. With multithreaded stepping, filter calls may run concurrently. Protect shared mutable data. Dynamic tree filter world.DynamicTree.Filter has this type: public Func<IDynamicTreeProxy, IDynamicTreeProxy, bool> Filter { get; set; } Its default is World.DefaultDynamicTreeFilter, which excludes shapes attached to the same body: public static bool DefaultDynamicTreeFilter(IDynamicTreeProxy proxyA, IDynamicTreeProxy proxyB) { if (proxyA is RigidBodyShape rbsA && proxyB is RigidBodyShape rbsB) { return rbsA.RigidBody != rbsB.RigidBody; } return true; } Pairs rejected here are not passed to either of the later filters. For soft bodies, another collision filter is typically used (defined in SoftBodies.DynamicTreeCollisionFilter.Filter), which also filters out collisions between shapes belonging to the same soft body. Broad phase filter world.BroadPhaseFilter is optional: public IBroadPhaseFilter? BroadPhaseFilter { get; set; } The default is null. When assigned, it receives pairs whose bounding boxes overlap. Return false to skip the shape collision test. If you add custom objects to world.DynamicTree, handle their collisions in this filter and return false for those pairs. The world's built-in collision detection only handles RigidBodyShape pairs; passing other types to it throws InvalidCollisionTypeException. Soft bodies use this approach through SoftBodies.BroadPhaseCollisionFilter. Example: Collision groups This filter lets members of the same team collide, while ignoring collisions between red and blue. Bodies without a team collide normally: public class TeamFilter : IBroadPhaseFilter { public class TeamMember { } public static TeamMember TeamRed = new(); public static TeamMember TeamBlue = new(); public bool Filter(IDynamicTreeProxy proxyA, IDynamicTreeProxy proxyB) { if (proxyA is not RigidBodyShape shapeA || proxyB is not RigidBodyShape shapeB) { return true; } if (shapeA.RigidBody.Tag is not TeamMember || shapeB.RigidBody.Tag is not TeamMember) { // Handle collision normally if at least one body is not a member of any team return true; } // There is no collision between team red and team blue. return shapeA.RigidBody.Tag == shapeB.RigidBody.Tag; } } The TeamFilter class can then be instantiated and assigned to world.BroadPhaseFilter: world.BroadPhaseFilter = new TeamFilter(); ... bodyA.Tag = TeamFilter.TeamBlue; bodyB.Tag = TeamFilter.TeamRed; bodyC.Tag = TeamFilter.TeamRed; Narrow phase filter world.NarrowPhaseFilter receives the detected contact: public INarrowPhaseFilter? NarrowPhaseFilter { get; set; } The callback receives contact points, a normal, and penetration depth. Return false to reject the collision, or modify the points and normal before returning true to keep it. Changing penetration depth alone does not change the contact response. The default, TriangleEdgeCollisionFilter, reduces snagging at edges shared by neighboring TriangleShapes. Without it, an object sliding across a flat mesh can catch on an edge between two triangles. Static and kinematic triangle bodies receive edge filtering. For dynamic triangle bodies, edge filtering is disabled by default to avoid destabilizing moving meshes. Enable it explicitly with FilterDynamicBodies: world.NarrowPhaseFilter = new TriangleEdgeCollisionFilter { FilterDynamicBodies = true };

docs/documentation/general.html.title: General | Jitter2
docs/documentation/general.html.summary: General This page covers collision detection, precision, repeatable simulations, and math conventions. Collision Detection Philosophy Jitter2 uses the same collision algorithms for all convex shapes. Each shape provides a support function: given a direction, it returns the furthest point in that direction. This is enough for a custom shape to collide with the built-in shapes. You do not need to write a separate collision test for each shape pair. Collision detection has two stages. The broad phase finds pairs whose bounding boxes overlap. The narrow phase tests the shapes in each pair and calculates contact points. Jitter2 uses MPR (Minkowski Portal Refinement), with EPA (Expanding Polytope Algorithm) for deeper overlaps. For large environments, collision filters let you supply geometry as needed. For example, a filter can generate nearby triangles from a heightmap or voxel world without adding the entire environment to the simulation. Precision Jitter2 supports both single-precision (float) and double-precision (double) floating-point arithmetic, selected at compile time. To build with double precision, either uncomment #define USE_DOUBLE_PRECISION in Precision.cs, or use the command line option: dotnet build -c Release -p:DoublePrecision=true The active precision mode can be checked at runtime via Precision.IsDoublePrecision. In single precision, JVector.X is a float; in double precision, it is a double. Build Configuration and Validation Jitter2 checks setup values such as shape dimensions, masses, constraint axes, and limits. Invalid values throw .NET exceptions in both Debug and Release builds. Debug builds also check changes to positions, velocities, forces, and orientations. These extra checks catch values such as infinity, NaN, or a quaternion that is not normalized. NuGet packages use Release builds. To get the extra Debug checks, build Jitter2 from source in the Debug configuration. Deterministic Simulation Jitter2 provides an optional cross-platform deterministic solver mode via SolveMode: world.SolveMode = SolveMode.Deterministic; Deterministic mode produces repeatable results across platforms when you use the same Jitter2 version, precision, time steps, and inputs. This is useful for tests, replays, and debugging. The creation order matters within each island, a group of bodies connected through contacts or constraints. Add the participating bodies, shapes, and constraints in the same order on every run. Unrelated parts of the world can be created in a different order. Solver configuration Repeatability SolveMode.Deterministic Designed to give the same results across platforms and thread counts when the setup and inputs above match. SolveMode.Regular with multiThread: false Repeating the exact same setup within one .NET process may give the same results. This is not a cross-platform guarantee. SolveMode.Regular with multiThread: true Results may vary between runs because the processing order can change. Float and double builds do not produce identical results, and results may change between Jitter2 versions. Note Cross-platform determinism is tested in CI on Linux x64, Windows x64, and macOS arm64. These tests support the claim for the configurations they cover; they cannot establish it for every possible scene or platform. Deterministic mode can be significantly slower. SolveMode.Regular remains the default for applications that do not need repeatable results. Coordinate System Jitter2's vector and rotation math uses a right-handed coordinate system. You can choose which axis points up. Gravity defaults to (0, -9.81, 0), so the default is Y-up. For a Z-up scene, change it to: world.Gravity = new JVector(0, 0, -9.81f); // Z-up convention Tracing and Logging Use logging to receive engine messages and tracing to investigate performance. Logging To receive Information, Warning, and Error messages, assign a listener: Logger.Listener = (level, message) => { Console.WriteLine($"[{level}] {message}"); }; The engine logs warnings for events such as EPA convergence issues or memory allocation fallbacks. Performance Tracing Build Jitter2 with the PROFILE symbol to record how long collision detection, constraint solving, and other parts of each step take. To export the recorded data: Tracer.WriteToFile("trace.json"); The output file uses the Chrome Trace Event format and can be visualized in: chrome://tracing (paste in Chrome's address bar) Perfetto UI Without PROFILE, tracing calls are omitted from the build and have no runtime cost. Custom Math Types Jitter2 uses JVector, JMatrix, JSymmetricMatrix, JQuaternion, and JBoundingBox. Their components use float or double, depending on the library's precision setting. The UnsafeAs and UnsafeFrom methods convert between Jitter2 types and other types with the same memory layout: // Convert to any layout-compatible type MyVector3 myVec = jitterVector.UnsafeAs<MyVector3>(); // Convert from any layout-compatible type JVector jitterVector = JVector.UnsafeFrom(myVec); Both types must have the same size and field layout. For System.Numerics, ordinary implicit conversions are also available: System.Numerics.Vector3 sysVec = jitterVector; // implicit conversion JVector jitterVec = sysVec; // implicit conversion Implicit conversions copy the component values. Converting from double to float can lose precision. Vector and matrix convention Jitter2 treats vectors as column vectors. To transform a vector \(v\) by a matrix \(M\), it calculates \(M \cdot v\): JVector result = JVector.Transform(v, M); // computes M * v System.Numerics uses row vectors and calculates \(v \cdot M\). Transpose matrices when converting between these conventions. In memory, JMatrix stores columns together (M11, M21, M31), while System.Numerics.Matrix4x4 stores rows together.

docs/documentation/shapes.html.title: Shapes | Jitter2
docs/documentation/shapes.html.summary: Shapes Shapes define the convex geometry used for collisions. Attach them to a rigid body with body.AddShape; the body supplies their position and rotation. Each shape implements ISupportMappable, so it can also be used directly in NarrowPhase collision queries. Shapes implement IDynamicTreeProxy as well, allowing the dynamic tree to track them. Adding a shape to a body registers it in world.DynamicTree automatically. Note Concave Shapes A concave shape can be represented by combining multiple convex shapes on a single rigid body. Third-party libraries for 'convex decomposition' can be used to generate convex hulls from arbitrary meshes. Changing an attached shape After changing an attached shape's dimensions or local transform, update its collision bounds, cached contacts, and, if needed, the body's mass properties. Do this between calls to world.Step: box.Size = new JVector(2, 1, 1); world.DynamicTree.Update(box); // Refresh this shape's bounding box and broadphase pairs. body.ClearContactCache(); // Discard contact points based on the old geometry. body.SetMassInertia(); // Only if the body uses mass properties derived from its shapes. world.DynamicTree.Update(shape) refreshes that shape immediately, even if its body is asleep. A regular world step only updates active objects. Wake a changed dynamic body with body.SetActivationState(true). If changing static geometry creates new overlaps with sleeping bodies, wake those bodies yourself. Resizing a shape can leave it overlapping other bodies. Decide whether to reposition those bodies or let the solver separate them. If you set mass or inertia manually, decide whether to keep or recalculate those values; SetMassInertia() without arguments replaces them with values derived from the shapes. Default types The inheritance hierarchy for the default shapes: Shape ├── RigidBodyShape │ ├── BoxShape │ ├── CapsuleShape │ ├── ConeShape │ ├── ConvexHullShape │ ├── CylinderShape │ ├── PointCloudShape │ ├── TransformedShape │ └── TriangleShape └── SoftBodyShape ├── SoftBodyTetrahedron └── SoftBodyTriangle The API reference describes each shape's dimensions and options. The following types need a little more setup. ConvexHullShape The constructor of the ConvexHullShape takes a list of triangles. public ConvexHullShape(List<JTriangle> triangles) The triangles must form a valid convex hull. Jitter2 rejects zero-mass hulls but does not fully validate the mesh. Invalid input can cause incorrect collisions or collision tests that fail to finish. Use convexHullShape.Clone() when several bodies need the same geometry. Each clone is a separate shape instance that shares the hull data. PointCloudShape The PointCloudShape is very similar to the ConvexHullShape. The constructor takes a list of vertices. public PointCloudShape(List<JVector> vertices) Jitter2 uses the convex hull of the supplied points: imagine stretching a tight skin around them. Points inside that hull do not change the collision shape. For example, the eight corners of a cube define a cube; adding a point at its center changes nothing. Warning Number of vertices PointCloudShapes should only be used for a small to moderate number of vertices (\(\approx{}300\)). Larger numbers of vertices can negatively impact performance. ConvexHullShapes are the better choice for more complex hulls. TransformedShape The TransformedShape takes another shape as input and transforms it. public TransformedShape(RigidBodyShape shape, in JVector translation, in JMatrix transform) Any affine transformation is possible. The wrapped shape might be translated, rotated, scaled and sheared. For example, a sphere shape could be transformed into an ellipsoid. TriangleShape The TriangleShape has no volume. It is mostly used for static geometry, although it can be added to non-static bodies. The TriangleShape is constructed with a TriangleMesh and an index. public TriangleShape(TriangleMesh mesh, int index) The mesh records which triangles share edges. TriangleEdgeCollisionFilter, enabled by default, uses this information to reduce snagging when bodies slide across those edges. SoftBodyShape A soft-body triangle or tetrahedron uses a separate rigid body for each vertex. Its geometry changes as those bodies move. Add it to a SoftBody, rather than attaching it to one rigid body. Debug drawing Shapes can be drawn individually: var shape = new SphereShape(radius: 1); shape.DebugDraw(drawer); Attached shapes follow their body's position and rotation. The sphere above appears at the world origin until it is attached to a body. See debugging shapes on a body for setting up the drawer and adjusting color and smoothness. Your drawer's DrawTriangle implementation chooses filled triangles or wireframes. See IDebugDrawer for the drawing methods. Warning Debug drawing can be slow. Point clouds and custom shapes may appear with gaps or overlapping faces. Higher detail settings increase the cost and do not guarantee a more accurate drawing. Custom shapes To define a custom convex shape, implement its support function: given a direction, return the point furthest in that direction. GetCenter must return a point inside the shape. All coordinates are local to the shape. This example defines a half-sphere with radius 1, aligned with the Y axis: public class HalfSphereShape : RigidBodyShape { public override void SupportMap(in JVector direction, out JVector result) { const float centerOfMassOffset = 3.0f / 8.0f; if (direction.Y >= 0.0f) { result = JVector.Normalize(direction); } else { JVector pDir = new JVector(direction.X, 0.0f, direction.Z); float pDirSq = pDir.LengthSquared(); if (pDirSq < 1e-12f) result = JVector.Zero; else result = (1.0f / MathF.Sqrt(pDirSq)) * pDir; } // shift, such that (0, 0, 0) is the center of mass result.Y -= centerOfMassOffset; } public override void GetCenter(out JVector point) { point = JVector.Zero; } } The default implementation calculates bounding boxes and approximates mass properties from the support function. Override these methods if you can provide faster or more accurate calculations, or a custom ray test: public override void CalculateBoundingBox(in JQuaternion orientation, in JVector position, out JBoundingBox box) public override void CalculateMassInertia(out JSymmetricMatrix inertia, out JVector com, out float mass) public override bool LocalRayCast(in JVector origin, in JVector direction, out JVector normal, out float lambda) The ShapeHelper class can also be used to generate a triangle mesh representation of the shape (or any class implementing ISupportMappable): public static List<JTriangle> Tessellate(ISupportMappable support, int subdivisions = 3)

docs/documentation/world.html.title: Jitter World | Jitter2
docs/documentation/world.html.summary: Jitter World A World contains the bodies, contacts, and constraints in a simulation. Call world.Step to advance it. World.Step Advance the simulation by dt seconds: Step(float dt, bool multiThread = true) Time step size Note Units in Jitter2 The unit system is not explicitly defined. The engine is optimized for objects with a size of 1 [len_unit]. For example, the collision system uses length thresholds on the order of 1e-04 [len_unit]. It assumes a unit density of 1 [mass_unit/len_unit³] for mass properties of shapes. Consequently, the default mass of a unit cube is 1 [mass_unit]. The default value for gravity is 9.81 [len_unit/time_unit²], which aligns with the gravitational acceleration on Earth in metric units (m/s²). Therefore, it is reasonable to use metric units (kg, m, s) when conceptualizing these values. Use a fixed time step of 1/60 second or less. Smaller steps generally improve stability but require more work for the same amount of simulated time. The following example accumulates elapsed time and advances physics in fixed 1/100-second steps. maxSteps limits the number of physics steps performed in one call if the application falls behind. private float accumulatedTime = 0.0f; public void FixedTimeStep(float dt, int maxSteps = 4) { const float fixedStep = 1.0f / 100.0f; int steps = 0; accumulatedTime += dt; while (accumulatedTime >= fixedStep) { world.Step(fixedStep); accumulatedTime -= fixedStep; // we cannot keep up with real time, i.e. the simulation // is running slower than the real time is passing. if (++steps >= maxSteps) return; } } Multithreading world.Step uses multiple threads by default. Jitter2's thread count includes the thread calling Step, so a count of four means that thread plus three workers. The default count is calculated by: public const float ThreadsPerProcessor = 0.9f; public static int ThreadCountSuggestion => Math.Max((int)(Environment.ProcessorCount * ThreadsPerProcessor), 1); To change the count for the shared thread pool: Jitter2.Parallelization.ThreadPool.Instance.ChangeThreadCount(4); This selects four threads in total. world.ThreadModel controls what workers do between steps. The default, ThreadModelType.Regular, lets them wait without consuming CPU time. ThreadModelType.Persistent keeps them active to reduce the delay before the next step, at the cost of higher CPU usage. Threading Contract Do not step or modify the same world from multiple threads at once. Also avoid reading its state while another thread is stepping or changing it. To simulate independent worlds in parallel, run each on a separate application thread and use single-threaded stepping: world.Step(dt, multiThread: false); world.Stabilize(dt, iterations, multiThread: false); Multithreaded calls to Step and Stabilize share one worker pool. If different worlds make these calls at the same time, one runs while the others wait. Any callbacks shared by worlds running concurrently must be thread-safe. This includes logging, collision filters, and event handlers. The same applies if your application draws debug geometry from multiple threads. Solver Mode Jitter2 offers two solver strategies through SolveMode: world.SolveMode = SolveMode.Regular; // default world.SolveMode = SolveMode.Deterministic; // reproducible, slower SolveMode.Regular favors speed. With multithreading, the order in which contacts and constraints are solved can vary between runs. SolveMode.Deterministic favors repeatable results and can be significantly slower. It supports both single-threaded and multithreaded stepping. Use deterministic mode for tests, replays, or applications that need the same inputs to produce the same result. The engine version, precision, time steps, inputs, and creation order of interacting bodies must match. See Deterministic Simulation for the full requirements and test coverage. Solver Iterations Jitter2 solves contacts and constraints through repeated adjustments to body velocities. More iterations generally make contacts and joints more accurate, at a higher cost: world.SolverIterations = (solver: 6, relaxation: 4); solver sets the number of iterations used to resolve contacts and constraints. These iterations also add motion to separate overlapping bodies and correct joint positions. relaxation sets the number of iterations used afterward to remove unwanted velocity introduced by those position corrections. Solving time grows roughly in proportion to the total number of iterations. Substep Count world.SubstepCount divides each simulation step into smaller steps. Each substep updates body motion and solves contacts and constraints. Existing contact points follow the moving bodies, but collision detection is not rerun to find new contacts. Each substep uses the iteration counts in world.SolverIterations. For example: world.SubstepCount = 4; world.SolverIterations = (solver: 2, relaxation: 1); This performs eight solver iterations and four relaxation iterations per call to world.Step. Substeps usually cost more than putting the same number of iterations into one step, but can give better results for joints, large stacks, and heavy objects resting on light ones. Contact Manifold Persistence By default, Jitter2 reuses contact points and impulses from the previous step (world.PersistentContactManifold = true). This gives the solver a useful starting point and helps resting objects stay stable. The set of contact points between two shapes is called a contact manifold. Set world.PersistentContactManifold = false to discard contacts after each step. Rebuilding them from scratch can require more solver iterations to achieve the same stability. Individual bodies can discard their cached contacts without changing the global setting: body.ClearContactCache(); // discard cached manifold for this body This is useful after restoring low-level body data. Setting body.Position or body.Orientation already clears the contact cache in both solver modes. Warm-Start Reset Constraints reuse impulses from the previous step, a technique called warm starting. After loading a saved state or making a sudden change to the bodies, those impulses may no longer be appropriate. Call ResetWarmStart() to clear them without removing the constraints: foreach (var constraint in body.Constraints) { constraint.ResetWarmStart(); } World.Stabilize can then adjust velocities to satisfy the restored contacts and constraints before simulation resumes. It does not advance body positions or orientations, and it uses the selected solver mode. Auxiliary Contacts When flat surfaces touch, one contact point may not be enough to keep them stable. Auxiliary contacts add more points during the same collision test, so the solver can support the touching surfaces without waiting several steps to collect more contacts. This is enabled by default. Set world.EnableAuxiliaryContactPoints = false to disable it. Rigid Bodies All rigid bodies registered with the world can be accessed using world.RigidBodies where RigidBodies is of type ReadOnlyPartitionedSet<RigidBody>. The bodies are in no particular order and may be reordered during calls to world.Step. Raw Data For low-level access to body, contact, and constraint data, use: world.RawData This provides spans over RigidBodyData, ContactData, ConstraintData, and SmallConstraintData. Most applications should use the properties on bodies, arbiters, and constraints instead. Caution Raw Memory Access Do not retain spans or data references across calls to Step or changes to the world: the underlying storage can move. Do not access raw data while another thread is stepping or modifying the world. Direct field changes bypass normal updates, such as refreshing collision bounds, and can leave the simulation in an invalid state. Warning Accessing Removed Entities Removing a body or constraint makes its simulation data unavailable. Check IsValid before using a reference that may have been removed. Do not retain an arbiter after EndCollide or explicit removal; it may be reused for a different collision. Removing Entities Rigid bodies, constraints, and shapes can be removed from the world: world.Remove(body); // removes body and its shapes world.Remove(constraint); // removes a constraint world.Clear(); // removes all entities Removing a body also removes its shapes, contacts, and attached constraints. Check constraint.IsValid before using a constraint whose body may have been removed. Changing body motion types suspends a constraint while neither body is dynamic; it does not remove the constraint. See Constraint lifetime. NullBody The world provides a special static body world.NullBody that is pinned to the world. It can be used to create constraints that fix a body relative to world space (see Constraints). Deactivation The deactivation system can be globally disabled using world.AllowDeactivation. Setting this to false prevents bodies from being deactivated but does not wake up already sleeping bodies. Jitter2 puts connected groups of bodies, called islands, to sleep together. An island can sleep once all of its non-static bodies have stayed below their velocity thresholds for long enough. See body activation for the thresholds and controls. Sleeping islands have very little simulation cost. They wake when your code activates a body, or when contact or a constraint connects them to active bodies. Static bodies do not keep an island awake. Moving static geometry can still wake the bodies affected by the change.

docs/introduction.html.summary: Jitter2 documentation Learn to build a simulation with Jitter2, then explore the engine's bodies, shapes, and constraints. Use the navigation on the left to browse the tutorials and reference guides. Start with a tutorial Falling boxes — Set up a .NET project, add a render loop, and simulate your first falling boxes. Teapot stacking — Load convex hulls and build a tower of teapots. Two boxes and a hinge — Connect bodies with a joint and render the scene through Jitter's debug drawer. Understand the engine General concepts: collision detection, precision, determinism, and math conventions. World: create and step a simulation. Rigid bodies and shapes: define the objects in your world. Constraints: connect bodies and restrict their motion.
