docs/tutorials/boxes/hello-world.html.title: Hello World | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/boxes/hello-world.html.summary: Hello World Now add a World to simulate the scene, a static body for the ground, and dynamic bodies for the boxes. Replace the contents of Program.cs with the following code. The highlighted lines add the physics: using System.Numerics; using Raylib_cs; using Jitter2; using Jitter2.Collision.Shapes; using Jitter2.Dynamics; using Jitter2.LinearMath; using static Raylib_cs.Raylib; static Matrix4x4 GetRayLibTransformMatrix(RigidBody body) { JMatrix ori = JMatrix.CreateFromQuaternion(body.Orientation); JVector pos = body.Position; return new Matrix4x4(ori.M11, ori.M12, ori.M13, pos.X, ori.M21, ori.M22, ori.M23, pos.Y, ori.M31, ori.M32, ori.M33, pos.Z, 0, 0, 0, 1.0f); } static Texture2D GenCheckedTexture(int size, int checks, Color colorA, Color colorB) { Image imageMag = GenImageChecked(size, size, checks, checks, colorA, colorB); Texture2D textureMag = LoadTextureFromImage(imageMag); UnloadImage(imageMag); return textureMag; } const int NumberOfBoxes = 12; // set a hint for anti-aliasing SetConfigFlags(ConfigFlags.Msaa4xHint); // initialize a 1200x800 px window with a title InitWindow(1200, 800, "BoxDrop example"); // dynamically create a plane model Texture2D texture = GenCheckedTexture(10, 1, Color.LightGray, Color.Gray); Model planeModel = LoadModelFromMesh(GenMeshPlane(10, 10, 10, 10)); SetMaterialTexture(ref planeModel, 0, MaterialMapIndex.Diffuse, ref texture); // dynamically create a box model texture = GenCheckedTexture(2, 1, Color.White, Color.Magenta); Mesh boxMesh = GenMeshCube(1, 1, 1); Material boxMat = LoadMaterialDefault(); SetMaterialTexture(ref boxMat, MaterialMapIndex.Diffuse, texture); // initialize the Jitter physics world World world = new(); world.SubstepCount = 4; // add a body representing the plane RigidBody planeBody = world.CreateRigidBody(); planeBody.AddShape(new BoxShape(10)); planeBody.Position = new JVector(0, -5, 0); planeBody.MotionType = MotionType.Static; // add NumberOfBoxes cubes for (int i = 0; i < NumberOfBoxes; i++) { RigidBody body = world.CreateRigidBody(); body.AddShape(new BoxShape(1)); body.Position = new JVector(0, i * 2 + 0.5f, 0); } // create a camera Camera3D camera = new() { Position = new Vector3(-20.0f, 8.0f, 10.0f), Target = new Vector3(0.0f, 4.0f, 0.0f), Up = new Vector3(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f), FovY = 45.0f, Projection = CameraProjection.Perspective }; // 100 fps target SetTargetFPS(100); // simple render loop while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(Color.Blue); BeginMode3D(camera); DrawModel(planeModel, Vector3.Zero, 1.0f, Color.White); world.Step(1.0f / 100.0f, true); foreach (var body in world.RigidBodies) { if (body == planeBody || body == world.NullBody) continue; // do not draw this DrawMesh(boxMesh, boxMat, GetRayLibTransformMatrix(body)); } EndMode3D(); DrawText($"{GetFPS()} fps", 10, 10, 20, Color.White); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); Run the program to see boxes fall onto the ground.

docs/tutorials/boxes/project-setup.html.title: Project Setup | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/boxes/project-setup.html.summary: Project Setup In this tutorial, you will use Raylib for rendering and Jitter for physics to make boxes fall onto the ground. Requirements Install the .NET 10 SDK. Check that the SDK is installed: dotnet --version Create a New Console Application and Add Jitter and Raylib First, create a new directory named "BoxDrop" and navigate into it: mkdir BoxDrop && cd BoxDrop Create a console application and add Raylib-cs and Jitter2: dotnet new console dotnet add package Raylib-cs --version 6.1.1 dotnet add package Jitter2 Run the application: dotnet run The console should print Hello, World!.

docs/tutorials/boxes/render-loop.html.title: Render Loop | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/boxes/render-loop.html.summary: Render Loop Start with a Raylib window, a camera, and a ground plane. Replace the contents of Program.cs with: using System.Numerics; using Raylib_cs; using static Raylib_cs.Raylib; static Texture2D GenCheckedTexture(int size, int checks, Color colorA, Color colorB) { Image imageMag = GenImageChecked(size, size, checks, checks, colorA, colorB); Texture2D textureMag = LoadTextureFromImage(imageMag); UnloadImage(imageMag); return textureMag; } // set a hint for anti-aliasing SetConfigFlags(ConfigFlags.Msaa4xHint); // initialize a 1200x800 px window with a title InitWindow(1200, 800, "BoxDrop example"); // dynamically create a plane model Texture2D texture = GenCheckedTexture(10, 1, Color.LightGray, Color.Gray); Model planeModel = LoadModelFromMesh(GenMeshPlane(10, 10, 10, 10)); SetMaterialTexture(ref planeModel, 0, MaterialMapIndex.Diffuse, ref texture); // create a camera Camera3D camera = new () { Position = new Vector3(-20.0f, 8.0f, 10.0f), Target = new Vector3(0.0f, 4.0f, 0.0f), Up = new Vector3(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f), FovY = 45.0f, Projection = CameraProjection.Perspective }; // 100 fps target SetTargetFPS(100); // simple render loop while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(Color.Blue); BeginMode3D(camera); DrawModel(planeModel, Vector3.Zero, 1.0f, Color.White); EndMode3D(); DrawText($"{GetFPS()} fps", 10, 10, 20, Color.White); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); Run the program to see the ground plane: Next, we will add falling boxes.

docs/tutorials/hinge/debug-drawer.html.title: Debug Drawer | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/hinge/debug-drawer.html.summary: Debug Drawer Jitter does not open a window or depend on a rendering library. Instead, objects that implement IDebugDrawable send geometry to an IDebugDrawer that you provide. For this example, the flow is: RigidBody.DebugDraw / HingeJoint.DebugDraw | v IDebugDrawer callbacks DrawSegment / DrawTriangle | v Raylib drawing calls Implement the two callbacks Our drawer renders segments as lines and triangles as filled surfaces. We draw the solid boxes first, then draw the hinge guides on top so the connection stays visible through the boxes. sealed class RaylibDebugDrawer : IDebugDrawer { public bool ShadeTriangles { get; init; } private static readonly Vector3 LightDirection = Vector3.Normalize(new(-1, 2, 3)); private static Vector3 ToVector(in JVector p) => new(p.X, p.Y, p.Z); private static Color ToColor(uint rgba) => new( (byte)((rgba >> 24) & 0xFF), (byte)((rgba >> 16) & 0xFF), (byte)((rgba >> 8) & 0xFF), (byte)(rgba & 0xFF)); public void DrawSegment(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, uint color) { DrawLine3D(ToVector(pA), ToVector(pB), ToColor(color)); } public void DrawTriangle(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, in JVector pC, uint color) { Vector3 a = ToVector(pA), b = ToVector(pB), c = ToVector(pC); Color tint = ToColor(color); // Simple face shading makes the solid boxes easier to read. Vector3 normal = Vector3.Cross(b - a, c - a); if (ShadeTriangles && normal.LengthSquared() > 0) { float light = 0.55f + 0.45f * Math.Max(0, Vector3.Dot(Vector3.Normalize(normal), LightDirection)); tint = new Color((byte)(tint.R * light), (byte)(tint.G * light), (byte)(tint.B * light), tint.A); } DrawTriangle3D(a, b, c, tint); } } There are three details to notice: Positions are already in world space. Convert JVector to Vector3 directly. Do not apply the body's position or orientation a second time. Colors are packed as 0xRRGGBBAA. The four shifts extract red, green, blue, and alpha explicitly, without depending on the machine's byte order. Both methods are required. Bodies emit triangles for their shape surfaces. Constraints emit segments and can also emit triangles for anchor markers and solid arrows. An empty DrawTriangle method would hide the boxes. ShadeTriangles adds a small amount of directional shading from each triangle's normal. This distinguishes the box faces without a shader or a separate mesh. It affects only the displayed color. We enable it for the bodies and leave it off for the joint's markers: var bodyDrawer = new RaylibDebugDrawer { ShadeTriangles = true }; var jointDrawer = new RaylibDebugDrawer(); Jitter emits counterclockwise front faces. Raylib uses their winding for back-face culling. The normal is calculated from that same vertex order. Choose colors and guide sizes var leftStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { CurrentColor = 0xFFD166FF }; var rightStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { CurrentColor = 0xFF997FFF }; var hingeStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { GuideSize = 0.65f, PointRadius = 0.04f, ArrowHeadSize = 0.1f, SolidArrows = false, ReferenceColor = 0x8CDBAAFF, CurrentColor = 0xFFD166FF }; CurrentColor colors each body's shape geometry. For the joint, ReferenceColor and CurrentColor distinguish its reference and current guides. The boxes are warm yellow and coral against the same blue background used in the other tutorials. The joint guides use green and gold, drawn on top of the filled boxes. GuideSize controls the angular guide radius in world units. PointRadius controls anchor markers separately. SolidArrows = false selects wire arrows. These settings affect only drawing: changing them does not change the hinge, mass, or collision shapes. Draw inside the camera's 3D pass BeginMode3D(camera); left.DebugDraw(bodyDrawer, leftStyle); right.DebugDraw(bodyDrawer, rightStyle); // Finish the solid geometry before changing the depth-test state. Rlgl.DrawRenderBatchActive(); Rlgl.DisableDepthTest(); hinge.DebugDraw(jointDrawer, hingeStyle); Rlgl.DrawRenderBatchActive(); Rlgl.EnableDepthTest(); EndMode3D(); The bodies draw their attached shapes in their current poses. The joint draws both of its constraints and automatically places the angular guide at the ball socket's anchor. The boxes use normal depth testing, so their visible faces cover surfaces behind them. For the joint pass, Rlgl.DisableDepthTest() lets the guides appear over the filled boxes, even where the guides are physically inside or behind them. This is a visualization overlay; it does not change collisions or the constraint. Raylib batches drawing commands. Rlgl.DrawRenderBatchActive() flushes the boxes before we disable depth testing, then flushes the guides before we restore it. Without those flushes, queued geometry could be drawn with the wrong depth-test state. Restore depth testing after the overlay so later 3D drawing behaves normally. The lines from the body centers to the anchor come from BallSocket. Its two anchor markers should stay close together. The circular guide and axis arrow come from HingeAngle. With a full angular range there are no stop markers; try the limit from the previous page to see them. Calling DebugDraw only draws the current state. world.Step advances the simulation. Next, Hello World brings these pieces together into a complete program and shows the hinge in motion. For more options, see Constraints, IDebugDrawer, and DebugDrawSettings.

docs/tutorials/hinge/hello-world.html.title: Hello World | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/hinge/hello-world.html.summary: Hello World Now put the scene, hinge, and debug drawer together. The yellow box stays fixed while gravity swings the coral box around their shared lower edge. The boxes are filled, with green and gold hinge guides drawn on top so the anchors, axis, and current angle stay visible. The recording holds the initial pose briefly, then runs the simulation. It loops back to the starting arrangement at the end. Complete code Using the project from Project Setup, replace Program.cs with the following. The RaylibDebugDrawer class belongs after the top-level statements in the same file. using System; using System.Numerics; using Jitter2; using Jitter2.Collision.Shapes; using Jitter2.Dynamics; using Jitter2.Dynamics.Constraints; using Jitter2.LinearMath; using Raylib_cs; using static Raylib_cs.Raylib; using World world = new(); world.Gravity = new JVector(0, -9.81f, 0); world.SubstepCount = 4; RigidBody left = world.CreateRigidBody(); left.AddShape(new BoxShape(2)); left.Position = new JVector(-1, 1, 0); left.MotionType = MotionType.Static; RigidBody right = world.CreateRigidBody(); right.AddShape(new BoxShape(2)); right.Position = new JVector(1, 1, 0); JVector hingeCenter = new(0, 0, 0); JVector hingeAxis = JVector.UnitZ; var hinge = new HingeJoint(world, left, right, hingeCenter, hingeAxis); var leftStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { CurrentColor = 0xFFD166FF }; var rightStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { CurrentColor = 0xFF997FFF }; var hingeStyle = new DebugDrawSettings { GuideSize = 0.65f, PointRadius = 0.04f, ArrowHeadSize = 0.1f, SolidArrows = false, ReferenceColor = 0x8CDBAAFF, CurrentColor = 0xFFD166FF }; SetConfigFlags(ConfigFlags.Msaa4xHint); InitWindow(1000, 750, "Jitter2 - Two boxes and a hinge"); SetTargetFPS(100); Camera3D camera = new() { Position = new Vector3(5, 3, 9), Target = new Vector3(0, -0.2f, 0), Up = Vector3.UnitY, FovY = 45, Projection = CameraProjection.Perspective }; var bodyDrawer = new RaylibDebugDrawer { ShadeTriangles = true }; var jointDrawer = new RaylibDebugDrawer(); bool paused = true; while (!WindowShouldClose()) { if (IsKeyPressed(KeyboardKey.Space)) paused = !paused; if (!paused) { world.Step(1.0f / 100.0f, true); } BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(Color.Blue); BeginMode3D(camera); left.DebugDraw(bodyDrawer, leftStyle); right.DebugDraw(bodyDrawer, rightStyle); // Finish the solid geometry before changing the depth-test state. Rlgl.DrawRenderBatchActive(); Rlgl.DisableDepthTest(); hinge.DebugDraw(jointDrawer, hingeStyle); Rlgl.DrawRenderBatchActive(); Rlgl.EnableDepthTest(); EndMode3D(); DrawText(paused ? "Paused - Space to release" : "Running - Space to pause", 20, 20, 22, Color.White); DrawText("Yellow: fixed box | Coral: dynamic box | Green / gold: hinge guides", 20, 52, 18, Color.White); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); sealed class RaylibDebugDrawer : IDebugDrawer { public bool ShadeTriangles { get; init; } private static readonly Vector3 LightDirection = Vector3.Normalize(new(-1, 2, 3)); private static Vector3 ToVector(in JVector p) => new(p.X, p.Y, p.Z); private static Color ToColor(uint rgba) => new( (byte)((rgba >> 24) & 0xFF), (byte)((rgba >> 16) & 0xFF), (byte)((rgba >> 8) & 0xFF), (byte)(rgba & 0xFF)); public void DrawSegment(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, uint color) { DrawLine3D(ToVector(pA), ToVector(pB), ToColor(color)); } public void DrawTriangle(in JVector pA, in JVector pB, in JVector pC, uint color) { Vector3 a = ToVector(pA), b = ToVector(pB), c = ToVector(pC); Color tint = ToColor(color); // Simple face shading makes the solid boxes easier to read. Vector3 normal = Vector3.Cross(b - a, c - a); if (ShadeTriangles && normal.LengthSquared() > 0) { float light = 0.55f + 0.45f * Math.Max(0, Vector3.Dot(Vector3.Normalize(normal), LightDirection)); tint = new Color((byte)(tint.R * light), (byte)(tint.G * light), (byte)(tint.B * light), tint.A); } DrawTriangle3D(a, b, c, tint); } } Run the example dotnet run The program starts paused so you can inspect the boxes and the hinge. Press Space to release the right box, and press it again to pause. Restart the program to return to the initial pose. Escape closes the window. Like the earlier tutorials, this example uses SetTargetFPS(100) and calls world.Step(1.0f / 100.0f, true) once per unpaused frame. Each step advances the simulation by 0.01 seconds; true enables Jitter's multithreaded stepping. This simple loop runs at real-time speed when it reaches 100 frames per second and slows down if rendering falls below that target. using World world releases Jitter's resources when the program exits. CloseWindow releases Raylib's window; this drawer owns no meshes or textures to unload. Try a limit Replace the HingeJoint construction with the limited version from Hinge Joint. The box will stop near a quarter turn, and the debug guides will show the allowed range. The drawer itself needs no changes.

docs/tutorials/hinge/hinge-joint.html.title: Hinge Joint | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/hinge/hinge-joint.html.summary: Hinge Joint Arrange the bodies first Both boxes are two units wide, high, and deep. With no initial rotation, their coordinates are: Left box Right box Center (-1, 1, 0) (1, 1, 0) X extent -2 to 0 0 to 2 Y extent 0 to 2 0 to 2 Z extent -1 to 1 -1 to 1 Motion Static Dynamic Their faces meet at x = 0. The lower edge of those faces is at x = 0, y = 0, running from z = -1 to z = 1. A point on that edge is the origin, and its direction is JVector.UnitZ. Create the world and bodies: using World world = new(); world.Gravity = new JVector(0, -9.81f, 0); world.SubstepCount = 4; RigidBody left = world.CreateRigidBody(); left.AddShape(new BoxShape(2)); left.Position = new JVector(-1, 1, 0); left.MotionType = MotionType.Static; RigidBody right = world.CreateRigidBody(); right.AddShape(new BoxShape(2)); right.Position = new JVector(1, 1, 0); BoxShape(2) specifies the full side length, not the half extent. Adding the shape gives the dynamic body its mass and inertia. A new body is dynamic by default; only the left body needs its motion type changed. The static box stays in place even though there is no ground or support beneath it. Gravity acts on the right box. Four solver substeps help keep the hinge anchors together as it swings. Attach the hinge JVector hingeCenter = new(0, 0, 0); JVector hingeAxis = JVector.UnitZ; var hinge = new HingeJoint(world, left, right, hingeCenter, hingeAxis); The anchor and axis are supplied in world coordinates. Create the joint after positioning the bodies: Jitter stores anchors and directions relative to them, using their initial pose as the reference. The axis is Z, even though the boxes are arranged along X. Rotation around Z lets the right box swing in the XY plane. An axis along X would describe a different connection. The right box's center of mass starts above and to the right of the anchor. Gravity therefore turns it clockwise in the front view shown above, while the left box stays fixed. There is no motor and no angular limit in this example. The bodies can still collide with each other; creating a hinge does not disable collision detection between them. What is inside a hinge? A free body has six degrees of freedom: three translations and three rotations. This hinge is a group of two constraints: Constraint What it does BallSocket Keeps the two anchor points together, removing three relative translations. HingeAngle Aligns the hinge axes, removing two relative rotations. One relative rotation remains, around Z. HingeJoint creates and initializes both constraints for you. They are accessible as hinge.BallSocket and hinge.HingeAngle. To construct the same connection explicitly, replace the HingeJoint construction with: var socket = world.CreateConstraint<BallSocket>(left, right); socket.Initialize(hingeCenter); var angle = world.CreateConstraint<HingeAngle>(left, right); angle.Initialize(hingeAxis, AngularLimit.Full); Do not add these on top of the joint: that would create duplicate constraints. The complete example keeps HingeJoint, which also gives us one object to draw. Try an angular limit later After running the example, replace the hinge construction with: var hinge = new HingeJoint(world, left, right, hingeCenter, hingeAxis, angle: AngularLimit.FromDegree(-90, 0)); The initial pose is zero. With this body order and the positive Z axis, downward rotation has a negative angle. This range lets the right box rotate down by about 90 degrees, then holds it near that limit. Constraints have finite stiffness and are solved iteratively, so small anchor separations or angular errors are normal. The debug drawing will also show the allowed angular range and its endpoints. Next, draw the bodies and joint and run the simulation.

docs/tutorials/hinge/project-setup.html.title: Project Setup | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/hinge/project-setup.html.summary: Project Setup Connect two boxes with a hinge and watch gravity swing one of them down. This tutorial introduces joints, the constraints inside them, and Jitter's debug drawing interface. The left box is fixed. The right box starts beside it along the X axis. Their hinge runs along the lower edge of the touching faces, parallel to the Z axis. We will draw the boxes and the hinge entirely through IDebugDrawer. Raylib supplies the window, camera, and drawing commands; Jitter supplies the geometry. No meshes, textures, or body transformation matrices are needed. Create the project Install the .NET 10 SDK, then create a console application: mkdir HingeDemo cd HingeDemo dotnet new console --framework net10.0 dotnet add package Jitter2 --version 2.13.0 dotnet add package Raylib-cs --version 6.1.1 This tutorial uses the colored IDebugDrawer API available in Jitter2 2.13.0. Both DrawSegment and DrawTriangle receive a packed color. What we will build Create the boxes and hinge, and understand the degrees of freedom it removes. Implement the debug drawer and connect it to Raylib. Run Hello World, with the complete code and a recording of the result. The complete Program.cs appears on the last page. The program starts paused so you can inspect the initial arrangement; press Space to release the right box or pause it again.

docs/tutorials/teapots/aftermath.html.title: Aftermath | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/teapots/aftermath.html.summary: Aftermath PointCloudShape vs ConvexHullShape The example uses PointCloudShape, which builds a convex collision shape from a set of points. Interior points are allowed, but do not change the shape. PointCloudShape is a good starting point for simple convex geometry. For more detailed models, ConvexHullShape can be faster. It requires triangles forming a valid, closed convex hull, which you must prepare with a tool such as Blender or a convex hull library. Jitter does not generate that mesh for you. As a rough guide, consider ConvexHullShape when the geometry has around 300 vertices or more. The crossover depends on the model, so measure your scene if collision performance matters.

docs/tutorials/teapots/hello-world.html.title: Hello World | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/teapots/hello-world.html.summary: Hello World Creating the PointCloudShape We can now create a PointCloudShape from the sampled vertices: // find a few points on the convex hull of the teapot. var vertices = ShapeHelper.SampleHull(allVertices, subdivisions: 3); // use these points to create a PointCloudShape. var pointCloudShape = new PointCloudShape(vertices); Jitter expects the body's center of mass at its local origin, (0, 0, 0). The teapot model is offset from that origin, so using it unchanged would make the body rotate around the wrong point. Use PointCloudShape.Shift to move the shape's center of mass to the origin: // find a few points on the convex hull of the teapot. var vertices = ShapeHelper.SampleHull(allVertices, subdivisions: 3); // use these points to create a PointCloudShape. var pointCloudShape = new PointCloudShape(vertices); // shift the shape so its center of mass is at the origin. pointCloudShape.GetCenter(out JVector centerOfMass); pointCloudShape.Shift = -centerOfMass; // pointCloudShape.GetCenter(out centerOfMass); // now returns (0, 0, 0) // finally, create the rigid body for the teapot var rigidBody = world.CreateRigidBody(); rigidBody.AddShape(pointCloudShape); Warning Apply the same shift when drawing the model, so the visible teapot matches its collision shape. The complete example below does this. Creating Multiple Instances of the Same Shape Each body needs its own shape instance. Use PointCloudShape.Clone() to create another instance that shares the same vertex data: var shapeInstance1 = new PointCloudShape(vertices); var shapeInstance2 = shapeInstance1.Clone(); // Safe to use in a second body This lets us reuse the sampled vertices for every teapot. Putting it all together Replace the contents of Program.cs with this complete example: using System.Numerics; using Raylib_cs; using Jitter2; using Jitter2.Collision.Shapes; using Jitter2.Dynamics; using Jitter2.LinearMath; using static Raylib_cs.Raylib; static Matrix4x4 GetRayLibTransformMatrix(RigidBody body) { JMatrix ori = JMatrix.CreateFromQuaternion(body.Orientation); JVector pos = body.Position; return new Matrix4x4(ori.M11, ori.M12, ori.M13, pos.X, ori.M21, ori.M22, ori.M23, pos.Y, ori.M31, ori.M32, ori.M33, pos.Z, 0, 0, 0, 1.0f); } static Texture2D GenCheckedTexture(int size, int checks, Color colorA, Color colorB) { Image imageMag = GenImageChecked(size, size, checks, checks, colorA, colorB); Texture2D textureMag = LoadTextureFromImage(imageMag); UnloadImage(imageMag); return textureMag; } const int numberOfTeapots = 12; // set a hint for anti-aliasing SetConfigFlags(ConfigFlags.Msaa4xHint); // initialize a 1200x800 px window with a title InitWindow(1200, 800, "TeaDrop example"); // dynamically create a plane model Texture2D texture = GenCheckedTexture(10, 1, Color.LightGray, Color.Gray); Model planeModel = LoadModelFromMesh(GenMeshPlane(20, 20, 10, 10)); SetMaterialTexture(ref planeModel, 0, MaterialMapIndex.Diffuse, ref texture); // load the teapot model from file Model teapotModel = LoadModel("teapot.obj"); // load the mesh vertices if (teapotModel.MeshCount == 0) throw new Exception("Model could not be loaded!"); Mesh teapotMesh; unsafe { teapotMesh = teapotModel.Meshes[0]; } var allVertices = teapotMesh.VerticesAs<JVector>(); // sample vertices on the convex hull var vertices = ShapeHelper.SampleHull(allVertices, 4); // create the PointCloudShape from the reduced vertices var pointCloudShape = new PointCloudShape(vertices); // shift the shape, such that the center of mass is at the origin pointCloudShape.GetCenter(out JVector center); pointCloudShape.Shift = -center; // we need to take the transpose here, since Raylib and System.Numerics // use a different convention Matrix4x4 shift = Matrix4x4.CreateTranslation(-center); shift = Matrix4x4.Transpose(shift); texture = GenCheckedTexture(16, 2, Color.White, Color.Magenta); Material teapotMat = LoadMaterialDefault(); SetMaterialTexture(ref teapotMat, MaterialMapIndex.Diffuse, texture); // initialize the Jitter physics world World world = new (); world.SubstepCount = 4; // add a body representing the plane RigidBody planeBody = world.CreateRigidBody(); planeBody.AddShape(new BoxShape(20)); planeBody.Position = new JVector(0, -10, 0); planeBody.MotionType = MotionType.Static; // add numberOfTeapots teapots for(int i = 0; i < numberOfTeapots; i++) { RigidBody body = world.CreateRigidBody(); body.AddShape(pointCloudShape.Clone()); body.Position = new JVector(0, i * 4 + 0.5f, 0); } // create a camera Camera3D camera = new () { Position = new Vector3(-40.0f, 16.0f, 20.0f), Target = new Vector3(0.0f, 4.0f, 0.0f), Up = new Vector3(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f), FovY = 45.0f, Projection = CameraProjection.Perspective }; // 100 fps target SetTargetFPS(100); // simple render loop while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(Color.Blue); BeginMode3D(camera); DrawModel(planeModel, Vector3.Zero, 1.0f, Color.White); world.Step(1.0f / 100.0f, true); foreach(var body in world.RigidBodies) { if (body == planeBody || body == world.NullBody) continue; // do not draw this DrawMesh(teapotMesh, teapotMat, GetRayLibTransformMatrix(body) * shift); } EndMode3D(); DrawText($"{GetFPS()} fps", 10, 10, 20, Color.White); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow();

docs/tutorials/teapots/hull-sampling.htm.title: Hull Sampling | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/teapots/hull-sampling.htm.summary: Hull Sampling The teapot has concave parts, such as the space under its handle. We will approximate it with a convex hull: imagine a tight skin stretched around the outside. The collision shape will not include those inward curves or holes. We can reduce collision detection work by keeping only some of the model's vertices. ShapeHelper.SampleHull selects outermost vertices in many directions. This removes interior points and gives us a smaller set that approximates the original hull. Fewer points are faster to test, but a coarser sample can lose detail. Replace the contents of Program.cs with: using System.Numerics; using Jitter2.Collision.Shapes; using Jitter2.LinearMath; using Raylib_cs; using static Raylib_cs.Raylib; // set a hint for anti-aliasing SetConfigFlags(ConfigFlags.Msaa4xHint); // initialize a 1200x800 px window with a title InitWindow(1200, 800, "TeaDrop example"); // load the teapot model from a file Model teapotModel = LoadModel("teapot.obj"); // load the mesh vertices if (teapotModel.MeshCount == 0) throw new Exception("Model could not be loaded!"); Mesh mesh; unsafe { mesh = teapotModel.Meshes[0]; } var allVertices = mesh.VerticesAs<JVector>(); var vertices = ShapeHelper.SampleHull(allVertices, 4); // just for visualization - // we will not need to construct the explicit hull for the simulation! var debugHull = ShapeHelper.Tessellate(vertices, 4); // create a camera Camera3D camera = new () { Position = new Vector3(-5.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f), Target = new Vector3(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f), Up = new Vector3(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f), FovY = 45.0f, Projection = CameraProjection.Perspective }; // 100 fps target SetTargetFPS(100); // simple render loop while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(Color.Blue); // make the scene rotate UpdateCamera(ref camera, CameraMode.Orbital); BeginMode3D(camera); // draw the teapot model DrawModelWires(teapotModel, Vector3.Zero, 1.0f, Color.White); // draw the sample vertices of the convex hull foreach (var vertex in vertices) { DrawSphere(vertex, 0.02f, Color.Red); } // for debugging: draw the explicit hull foreach (var vertex in debugHull) { DrawLine3D(vertex.V0, vertex.V1, Color.Green); DrawLine3D(vertex.V1, vertex.V2, Color.Green); DrawLine3D(vertex.V2, vertex.V0, Color.Green); } EndMode3D(); DrawText($"{GetFPS()} fps", 10, 10, 20, Color.White); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); White shows the model, green shows the approximate hull, and red dots mark the sampled vertices.

docs/tutorials/teapots/project-setup.htm.title: Project Setup | Jitter2
docs/tutorials/teapots/project-setup.htm.summary: Project Setup The Boxes tutorial used built-in shapes. This tutorial uses vertices from a model to create a collision shape for the Utah teapot. We will load teapot.obj, simplify its vertices, and stack several teapots in the simulation. Requirements Install the .NET 10 SDK. Check that the SDK is installed: dotnet --version Create a New Console Application and Add Jitter and Raylib First, create a new directory named "TeaDrop" and navigate into it: mkdir TeaDrop && cd TeaDrop Download and unzip the teapot.obj model. wget https://github.com/notgiven688/jitterphysics2/raw/refs/heads/main/src/JitterDemo/assets/teapot.obj.zip unzip teapot.obj.zip Create a console application and add Raylib-cs and Jitter2: dotnet new console dotnet add package Raylib-cs --version 6.1.1 dotnet add package Jitter2 Add these settings inside the <Project> element in TeaDrop.csproj. They allow access to Raylib's mesh data through pointers and copy teapot.obj to the output directory: <PropertyGroup> <AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <None Update="teapot.obj"> <CopyToOutputDirectory>Always</CopyToOutputDirectory> </None> </ItemGroup> Run the application: dotnet run The console should print Hello, World!.
